# Electromagnetic Vlasov–Maxwell kinetics {#sec-vlasov}

`apps/vlasov_maxwell` — a collisionless kinetic distribution function on a
three-dimensional phase space, coupled self-consistently to the full Maxwell
system, with a Lorentz cross-product force and electromagnetic instabilities.

Every other application in this report evolves a field over physical space.
This one evolves a *distribution over phase space*: the unknown is
$f_s(x, v_x, v_y, t)$, a function of one spatial and two velocity
coordinates, and the fields it is coupled to are three components of $E$ and
$B$ that live on the spatial line alone. The phase space is where the memory
goes and the coupling is where the physics is.

It is also the chapter where the reader meets a genuinely large system. That
is deliberate. @sec-alloy-dendrite showed that OpenPFC's finite-difference
and spectral stacks compose; this one shows that the framework survives a
problem whose unknown does not live on the grid the fields live on.

## Physical setting

A plasma is a gas in which the particles are charged, and that single change
makes it a field theory. Neutral gas molecules interact only when they
collide, so a neutral gas at low density is nearly a set of independent
particles. Charged particles interact through fields that every one of them
contributes to and every one of them feels, at every distance. A plasma is
therefore never a collection of particles in an external field; it is a
collection of particles in *its own* field, and that self-consistency is the
entire difficulty.

At the densities and temperatures where collisions can be neglected, the
statistical description is the **Vlasov equation**: the distribution function
$f_s(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}, t)$ is conserved along the trajectories of the
smooth, self-consistent field. Nothing is dissipated, nothing is lost, and
the entropy $-\int f \ln f$ is exactly constant. That makes the system
Hamiltonian in a strong sense — and it makes the two most famous phenomena in
the subject surprising.

**Landau damping** [@Landau1946]. A wave in a collisionless plasma decays. There is no
dissipation anywhere in the equations, entropy is exactly conserved, and yet
the electric field of a small perturbation dies away exponentially. The
energy is not lost; it goes into a progressively finer structure in velocity
space, carried by particles moving at close to the wave's phase velocity.
This is a real physical effect, it was predicted before it was measured, and
it is the sharpest test in this chapter because the damping rate is the root
of a transcendental equation that can be solved to machine precision and
compared against.

**Instability.** The same free energy that a Maxwellian has exhausted is
available whenever the distribution is *not* Maxwellian. Two counter-streaming
beams can give up their relative kinetic energy to a growing wave. Which wave
grows depends on the geometry, and the distinction matters here:

- Beams streaming **along** the wave vector drive a charge-density
  modulation. The unstable field is $E_x$, longitudinal; this is the
  electrostatic **two-stream** instability, and it is visible in a
  Vlasov–Poisson model with no magnetic field at all.
- Beams streaming **across** the wave vector drive a transverse current
  modulation. Current filaments of the same sign attract, the filaments
  coalesce, and the unstable field is a *magnetic* field $B_z$ that grows
  out of nothing. This is the **Weibel** [@Weibel1959], or filamentation, instability, and
  it cannot happen in an electrostatic model. It is why this application is
  electromagnetic and why it carries two velocity coordinates rather than
  one.

The second is the physically interesting case and the harder test. A model
that grows a magnetic field from a noise seed at the right rate has the
Lorentz force, the current deposition, the Maxwell update and the phase-space
transport all simultaneously correct; any one of them wrong and the growth
rate is wrong or the instability is absent.

## Governing equations

The complete system, presented before any reduction. For each species $s$
with charge $q_s$ and mass $m_s$:

$$
\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial t}
  + \mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f_s
  + \frac{q_s}{m_s}\left(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\right)
      \cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{v}} f_s = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-vlasov}

coupled to Maxwell's equations,

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},
\qquad
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0,
$$ {#eq-vm-gauss}

$$
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = -\nabla\times\mathbf{E},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}
  = c^{2}\nabla\times\mathbf{B} - \frac{\mathbf{J}}{\varepsilon_0},
$$ {#eq-vm-maxwell}

and closed by the kinetic moments

$$
\rho(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int f_s \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v},
\qquad
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v}.
$$ {#eq-vm-moments}

@eq-vm-vlasov is one equation per species on a six-dimensional phase space;
@eq-vm-maxwell is six scalar evolution equations on physical space;
@eq-vm-gauss is two constraints; @eq-vm-moments is the coupling that makes
the whole thing self-consistent and nonlinear. Written out in components for
several species it is a system of a few dozen coupled equations, and that is
before a single discretisation choice is made.

### The 1D2V reduction, derived

The application solves a reduction, and the reduction is *derived* here
rather than substituted, because which components survive is not obvious and
getting it wrong is silent.

Take one spatial coordinate $x$, two velocity coordinates $(v_x, v_y)$, and
let every field depend on $x$ and $t$ only, so $\partial_y = \partial_z = 0$.
The closure $f_s(x, v_x, v_y, t)$ carries no $v_z$, so $J_z \equiv 0$.
Under those two statements @eq-vm-gauss and @eq-vm-maxwell separate into
three groups.

**One component disappears for free.** $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ becomes
$\partial_x B_x = 0$, so $B_x$ is uniform in space; the $x$ component of
Faraday's law gives $\partial_t B_x = 0$, so it is uniform in time as well.
On a periodic line with $B_x(t=0) = 0$, therefore $B_x \equiv 0$ **exactly,
as an identity of the geometry**. This is worth stating clearly for a reason
that returns in @sec-vm-verification: it means $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0$ is
*not* a meaningful numerical test in this geometry, and reporting it as a
passed check would be misleading.

**One pair decouples.** The remaining Faraday and Ampère components pair
$(E_z, B_y)$ together,
$\partial_t B_y = \partial_x E_z$ and
$\partial_t E_z = c^2 \partial_x B_y$, driven by $J_z$ — which the closure
has set to zero. That pair is a vacuum electromagnetic wave the plasma cannot
touch. Initialised to zero it stays zero, and the application does not carry
it.

**What is left is the physics.** Three field components,

$$
\partial_x E_x = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
\qquad \text{(Gauss --- a constraint)}
$$ {#eq-vm-gauss1d}

$$
\frac{\partial E_x}{\partial t} = -\frac{J_x}{\varepsilon_0}
\qquad \text{(Ampère --- the evolution form of the same field)}
$$ {#eq-vm-ampere-x}

$$
\frac{\partial E_y}{\partial t} = -c^2\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial x}
   - \frac{J_y}{\varepsilon_0},
\qquad
\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial E_y}{\partial x} .
$$ {#eq-vm-transverse}

With $\mathbf{B} = B_z\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ and
$\mathbf{v} = (v_x, v_y, 0)$ the Lorentz force keeps its cross product
intact,

$$
(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})_x = +v_y B_z,
\qquad
(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B})_y = -v_x B_z,
$$ {#eq-vm-lorentz}

which rotates velocity vectors in the $(v_x, v_y)$ plane at the gyro-frequency
$\omega_c = q_s B_z / m_s$. **That rotation is the whole reason for two
velocity coordinates.** A 1D1V model has no cross product, no gyro-motion, no
transverse current and therefore no electromagnetic instability; it is a
different and much easier problem.

### Normalisation

Time in $\omega_{pe}^{-1}$, length in the electron skin depth
$d_e = c/\omega_{pe}$, velocity in $c$, $E$ in $m_e c\,\omega_{pe}/e$, $B$ in
$m_e\omega_{pe}/e$, and $f_s$ scaled so $\int f_s\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{v} =
n_s/n_0$. Then $c = \varepsilon_0 = 1$, and with $\sigma_s = q_s/(-e)$ and
$\mu_s = m_s/m_e$ the evolved system is

$$
\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial t}
 + v_x \frac{\partial f_s}{\partial x}
 + \frac{\sigma_s}{\mu_s}\left[
     \left(E_x + v_y B_z\right)\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial v_x}
   + \left(E_y - v_x B_z\right)\frac{\partial f_s}{\partial v_y}
   \right] = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-norm}

with @eq-vm-gauss1d–@eq-vm-transverse losing their $c$ and $\varepsilon_0$.
For electrons $\sigma_s = -1$, $\mu_s = 1$. The Debye length is
$\lambda_D = (v_{th}/c)\,d_e$, so electrostatic benchmarks quoted in
$k\lambda_D$ and electromagnetic ones quoted in $k d_e$ differ by the
thermal velocity in units of $c$.

### Gauss is a diagnostic, not a constraint to be imposed

@eq-vm-gauss1d and @eq-vm-ampere-x are two statements about the same field.
Differentiating the first in time and substituting the second,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\partial_x E_x - \rho\right)
  = -\left(\partial_x J_x + \partial_t \rho\right) = 0
$$ {#eq-vm-charge}

by the continuity equation, which is itself a moment of @eq-vm-vlasov.
**Gauss's law is preserved exactly if and only if the discrete scheme
conserves charge.** It is therefore not something to enforce and forget: it
is the sharpest available measurement of whether the transport and the
deposition are consistent with each other, and this application reports the
residual $\|\partial_x E_x - \rho\|_\infty/\|\rho\|_\infty$ at every
diagnostic sample of every run.

## Problem setup

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Use case | A collisionless electron plasma on a neutralising background, perturbed and allowed to evolve self-consistently with its own electromagnetic field. Five benchmark configurations, from a vacuum light wave to the Weibel instability |
| Domain | One OpenPFC 3-D `Domain` whose axes are $(x, v_x, v_y)$ — **the phase space is the grid.** $x$ spans $[0, L_x)$ in electron skin depths; $v_x$ and $v_y$ span $[-v_{\max}, +v_{\max}]$ in units of $c$ |
| Boundary conditions | $x$ **periodic**, physically. $v_x$, $v_y$ **not periodic**: zero inflow, and the distribution must be negligible at the boundary. The velocity boundary is the honest weak point of a structured-grid kinetic method, so the occupancy there is a reported diagnostic of every run rather than an assumption |
| Initial conditions | Analytic, in `ics.hpp`: Maxwellian, bi-Maxwellian, and two counter-streaming configurations that differ only in which velocity component carries the drift — along $k$ for the electrostatic two-stream case, across $k$ for the electromagnetic filamentation case |
| Key physical parameters | Per species $\sigma_s = q_s/(-e)$ and $\mu_s = m_s/m_e$; electrons are $(-1, 1)$. Thermal velocity $v_{th}/c$, drift $u/c$, box $L_x/d_e$, and the temperature ratio $A = T_y/T_x = (v_{th,y}/v_{th,x})^2$ for the Weibel case, which is unstable for $A > 1$. Ions are immobile by default and available as a second species behind a flag |
| Observables | Field energies $\tfrac12\int E_x^2$, $\tfrac12\int(E_y^2 + B_z^2)$; per-species particle number, momentum and kinetic energy; total energy; the Gauss residual; $\min f$; the $L^1$ and $L^2$ norms and the entropy $-\int f\ln f$; velocity-boundary occupancy |
| Model maturity | numerical verification: **analytical** — vacuum \(\omega=ck\) to round-off; Landau \(\gamma,\omega\), two-stream \(\gamma\) and Weibel \(\gamma(k)\) against a dispersion relation solved at run time (residuals at \(10^{-13}\)); gyro-frequency to \(3.6\times10^{-6}\); estimators tested on synthetic series, not only on the runs they report. physical completeness: **reduced** — 1D2V, non-relativistic, collisionless, immobile ions by default; the Lorentz cross product and Maxwell coupling are present, oblique Weibel modes are not. calibration: **none** — \(v/c\le 0.2\) is a regime, not a fitted plasma |

### Numerical strategy

Strang splitting in the manner of @Cheng1976, and the reason it works so cleanly here is a property
specific to 1D2V electromagnetic Vlasov: **every split step is a
constant-coefficient translation along one axis.**

| step | equation | speed | independent of | method |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | $\partial_t f + v_x\,\partial_x f = 0$ | $v_x$ | $x$ | exact spectral shift, $\hat f_k \mapsto \hat f_k e^{-\mathrm{i}k v_x \Delta t}$ |
| B | $\partial_t f + a_x\,\partial_{v_x} f = 0$ | $a_x = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}(E_x + v_y B_z)$ | $v_x$ | semi-Lagrangian, Lagrange interpolation |
| C | $\partial_t f + a_y\,\partial_{v_y} f = 0$ | $a_y = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}(E_y - v_x B_z)$ | $v_y$ | semi-Lagrangian, over the distributed axis |

Step A is exact and carries no timestep restriction, because $x$ is periodic
and the shift speed does not depend on the coordinate being shifted. Steps B
and C are constant-coefficient for the same reason — $a_x$ depends on $x$
and $v_y$ but not on $v_x$, and $a_y$ depends on $x$ and $v_x$ but not on
$v_y$ — so each is a pure translation, not a variable-coefficient advection.
That is a real simplification and it is worth being explicit that it is a
property of this geometry rather than a general fact about Vlasov solvers.

**The field update is exact too.** In Fourier space along $x$ the
source-free transverse pair of @eq-vm-transverse is

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
\begin{pmatrix}\hat E_y\\ \hat B_z\end{pmatrix}
= -\mathrm{i}k
\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\hat E_y\\ \hat B_z\end{pmatrix},
$$ {#eq-vm-rot}

whose matrix exponential is the closed form
$\cos(k\Delta t)\,\mathbf{I} - \mathrm{i}\sin(k\Delta t)\,\mathbf{S}$ with $\mathbf{S} = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
The light wave is therefore integrated **exactly, at any $\Delta t$**: it
carries no numerical dispersion and imposes no Courant condition, which for
an explicit electromagnetic solver is the restriction one would normally
expect to dominate. The current enters through Duhamel's formula, which is
the same exponential-time-differencing structure the spectral applications
of this report already use (@sec-etd).

What that leaves is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to present an
exact sub-step as though it made the method exact: the splitting is second
order, and **the real error of this application lives in the velocity-space
interpolation of steps B and C.** @sec-vm-verification measures it.

### Decomposition, and the cap it implies

The MPI decomposition is on $v_y$ **only**, and the consequences are the
reason for the choice:

- $x$ and $v_x$ are rank-local, so step A's transform is a local
  one-dimensional FFT needing no transpose, and step B is a purely local
  shift.
- Step C translates along the distributed axis and is served by the existing
  halo exchange, with width
  $\lceil \max|a_y|\,\Delta t/\Delta v_y\rceil + \tfrac12\,$(interpolation
  order). This is a Courant-like condition on the *velocity* step, checked at
  runtime: exceeding the halo is an error, never a silent wrap.
- $E_x$, $E_y$ and $B_z$ are one-dimensional in $x$ and cheap to replicate on
  every rank; the moments need one `MPI_Allreduce` per step over arrays of
  length $N_x$.
- **The rank count is capped at $N_{v_y}$.** That is a real limit of this
  decomposition and it is stated here rather than discovered during the
  scaling study. Going beyond it needs a second decomposition axis and a
  transpose, which is a larger change than this application justifies.

Memory is a first-class result rather than an implementation detail, and it
is the reason kinetic equations are expensive even though every operator in
@eq-vm-norm is first order: one species costs
$N_x N_{v_x} N_{v_y} \times 8$ bytes per working copy, so a
$1024\times512\times512$ phase space is 2.1 GB per copy before any field is
allocated. @sec-vm-scaling gives the measured figure.

## Verification {#sec-vm-verification}

Six rungs, each with an oracle that is not the code. Where a rung compares
against a dispersion relation, that relation is **solved numerically** by
`apps/common/include/openpfc_apps/plasma_dispersion.hpp`, whose own test
asserts that the residual $|D(\omega,k)|$ at the returned root is at
round-off. The plasma dispersion function itself follows @Weideman1994,
and the tabulated Landau roots of @Canosa1973 are used as a check on the
root-finder rather than as the oracle. No growth rate in this chapter is a remembered number.

### Stage 1: the vacuum electromagnetic wave

No plasma at all, so $\rho = \mathbf{J} = 0$ and only the field integrator
is under test.

| $N_x$ | 64 | 128 | 64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $\Delta t$ | 0.05 | 0.05 | **5.0** |
| energy drift over $t = 50$ | $9.4\times10^{-14}$ | $1.1\times10^{-13}$ | $1.2\times10^{-15}$ |

The third column is the point. A step of $5.0$ is a hundred times the step
the other two use and far beyond any Courant condition, and it is *more*
accurate — because there are fewer steps and each one is exact.
$\omega(k) = k$ holds to $1.9\times10^{-16}$ relative for all 31 resolved
modes. The light wave in this application carries no dispersion error and
imposes no timestep restriction at all.

### Stage 2: the electrostatic reduction

With `--electrostatic`, $E_y$ and $B_z$ are held at zero and $E_x$ comes
from Gauss. The reduction is exact as a code path: the transverse fields
remain identically zero, bitwise.

**Landau damping.** Maxwellian plus a 1 % density perturbation, compared
against the root of
$1 + (k\lambda_D)^{-2}[1 + \zeta Z(\zeta)] = 0$, with $Z$ the plasma
dispersion function [@Fried1961].

| $k\lambda_D$ | 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.5 | 0.6 | 0.8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $\gamma$ measured | −0.012686 | −0.066301 | −0.153753 | −0.264411 | −0.536250 |
| $\gamma$ oracle | −0.012620 | −0.066128 | −0.153359 | −0.264110 | −0.534552 |
| error | −0.52 % | −0.26 % | **−0.26 %** | −0.11 % | −0.32 % |
| $\omega$ error | +0.26 % | +0.11 % | −0.015 % | −0.065 % | −0.13 % |

: Landau damping against the numerically solved kinetic dispersion relation. {#tbl-vm-landau}

**Two-stream.** Counter-streaming along $\hat{x}$, growth of $E_x$:
measured $0.31908$ against $0.31994$, **−0.27 %**.

### Stage 3: the Lorentz force

Uniform imposed $B_z$, self-consistent fields off. The magnetic force does
no work, so the mean velocity must rotate rigidly at $\omega_c$.

| $B_z$ | 0.2 | 0.5 | 1.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| rotation rate error | $3.59\times10^{-6}$ | $3.64\times10^{-6}$ | $3.64\times10^{-6}$ |

This is the rung that catches a sign error in the cross product, and it
earned its place twice over: the first version of the *oracle* had the
wrong sign and reported a 200 % error on a rotation whose magnitude was
right to seven digits. $\mathrm{d}(v_x + \mathrm{i}v_y)/\mathrm{d}t =
-\mathrm{i}\,(q/m)B_z\,(v_x + \mathrm{i}v_y)$, so the phase advances at
$-(q/m)B_z$.

The same frozen-$B$ problem, with an $x$-independent drifting Maxwellian
so that `advect_x` is the identity, is the test of the Strang splitting
itself. Vacuum waves are exact at any $\Delta t$ and Landau $\gamma$ is
insensitive to the step, so neither measures the order. Against the
closed-form mean velocity over one gyro period, with
$\Delta t = T/\{8,16,32,64\}$, the fitted order is **2.07** (pairwise
2.17, 2.04, 2.02) and the finest error is smaller than the coarsest.

### Stage 4: electromagnetic instability

The rung the whole application exists for. Bi-Maxwellian with
$A = T_y/T_x = 9$, magnetic field growing out of a seeded mode, compared
against the transverse dispersion relation derived in
`plasma_dispersion.hpp`.

| $k\,d_e$ | 0.25 | 0.5 | 0.75 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 3.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| $\gamma$ measured | 0.030631 | 0.054657 | 0.069574 | 0.076068 | 0.071062 | — |
| $\gamma$ oracle | 0.030568 | 0.054592 | 0.069480 | 0.075977 | 0.070956 | 0 |
| error | +0.21 % | +0.12 % | +0.13 % | +0.12 % | +0.15 % | **no growth** |

: The Weibel instability across a sixfold range in wave number. {#tbl-vm-weibel}

The last column is as important as the other five. The marginal-stability
condition is $k^2c^2 = \omega_{pe}^2(A-1)$, so $k_c = \sqrt{A-1} = 2.83$,
and $k = 3$ must be **stable**. It is: the seeded mode decays. A model that
grew every mode it was given would match five growth rates and still be
wrong.

Cold counter-streaming filamentation, a different configuration reaching
the same instability: **+0.043 %**.

At higher resolution ($64\times128\times128$) the $k = 0.5$ case agrees to
**+0.0086 %**.

Five wave numbers agreeing to 0.2 % over a sixfold range is also the best
available evidence that the transverse relation is *correct*. It is the one
piece of this application derived rather than quoted — no readable primary
source in $Z$-function form could be obtained — and its provenance is the
derivation, two analytic limits (the cutoff of @Weibel1959 as $\zeta \to 0$,
and $\gamma \to \beta\omega_{pe}$ in the cold large-$k$ limit [@Bret2010]), and this
scan. A wrong relation does not track a simulation to a part in five
hundred across a scan.

### What actually limits the accuracy

Three scans were run to find out, and two of them found nothing — which is
how the third became conclusive.

| varied | range | effect on $\gamma$ |
|---|---|---|
| $N_{v_x}$ | 64 → 2048 | none beyond $2\times10^{-4}$ |
| interpolation order | 3 → 9 | none, while entropy drift fell $2.6\times10^{-8} \to 1.3\times10^{-12}$ |
| $\Delta t$ | 0.05 → 0.00625 | none, while energy drift fell as $\Delta t^2$ |
| $N_x$ | 16 → 128 | none at all |
| **$N_{v_y}$** | **8 → 32** | **−1.87 % → −0.26 %** |

: Only one axis mattered, and it was not one that had been scanned. {#tbl-vm-conv}

The defect was a velocity *spacing*, not an extent. The application already
refused a box too narrow to hold the distribution; it did not check whether
the grid inside the box could integrate it. By Poisson summation the
midpoint rule on a Gaussian is exact up to the aliased copies of its
transform, so the quadrature error is

$$
\varepsilon \;=\; 2\exp\!\left[-2\pi^2 \left(\frac{v_{th}}{\Delta v}\right)^{2}\right],
$$ {#eq-vm-quad}

which is $1.4\times10^{-2}$ at half a cell per thermal width,
$5\times10^{-9}$ at one, and $10^{-34}$ at two. The Landau runs had
$N_{v_y} = 8$ over $\pm 8 v_{th}$ — half a cell per thermal width — and
deposited a density 1.44 % low, exactly @eq-vm-quad's value. Every scan
that had been run varied $N_{v_x}$ while $N_{v_y}$ stayed at 8, so the
error was invisible to all of them and looked like an irreducible
"asymptotic versus finite-window" residual.

It was not. `require_resolved_spacing` now refuses such a grid on both
velocity axes and says in its message that it is not the same condition as
the tail check. The lesson generalises past this application: **a
convergence study that varies one axis of a multi-dimensional
discretisation can converge beautifully onto the wrong answer.**

### Conservation

Every run reports these every sample.

| quantity | typical drift | note |
|---|---|---|
| particle number | $10^{-14}$ | exact for the spectral shift, interpolation-limited for the others |
| total energy | $4\times10^{-8}$ at $\Delta t = 0.05$, falling as $\Delta t^{2}$ | kinetic and field parts exchange; only the sum is conserved |
| entropy | $5\times10^{-10}$ at order 5, $1.3\times10^{-12}$ at order 9 | conserved analytically, so this *is* the numerical diffusion |
| $\min f$ | $-7\times10^{-4}$ | Lagrange interpolation above first order is not positive; reported, never clipped |
| Gauss residual | $10^{-14}$ absolute | see below |

The Gauss residual deserves one remark. Its natural normalisation is
$\|\rho\|_\infty$, which is the right choice for an electrostatic run and a
$0/0$ for an electromagnetic one: a Weibel plasma stays neutral to
$10^{-5}$, so the relative form reads $0.27$ while the absolute residual is
$4\times10^{-6}$ against a field of $8\times10^{-2}$. Both are reported,
with the field scale alongside, so a reader can form the ratio that means
something for the run in front of them.

![The three linear benchmarks. Each oracle is the root of a dispersion relation solved numerically at run time, not a remembered number, and each dashed line is drawn only through the exponential phase — an oracle drawn across the plateau would invite the reader to see a disagreement that is the physics.](figures/vlasov_rates.svg){#fig-vm-rates}

## Nonlinear behaviour

### Electrostatic: phase-space vortices

![$f(x, v_x)$, integrated over $v_y$, through the two-stream instability. Two beams, a growing sinusoidal modulation, and then the roll-up into a phase-space vortex — trapped particles circulating in the potential well of the wave they created. The speckle in the last two panels is real: the vortex winds $f$ into filaments that thin without limit, and by $t = 63$ they are at the grid scale.](figures/vlasov_twostream_phase.svg){#fig-vm-twostream}

The two-stream instability saturates by **trapping**: the wave grows until
its potential well is deep enough to hold the particles that were driving
it, they begin to circulate rather than stream, and the free energy is
gone. @fig-vm-twostream is that sentence as a picture, and the vortex is
the standard signature.

It is also where the method's honest limit lives. The vortex winds $f$ into
ever thinner filaments in velocity — the Vlasov flow is incompressible in
phase space, so structure is never destroyed, only made finer — and no
fixed grid can follow that indefinitely. What happens instead is that the
interpolation smooths filaments at the grid scale, and the entropy, which
the continuous equation conserves exactly, begins to rise. That drift is
reported (@sec-vm-verification) precisely because it is the quantitative
statement of how much of the fine structure has been lost.

### Electromagnetic: filaments and the anisotropy that fed them

![$f(v_x, v_y)$ summed over $x$, at the start, during growth, and after saturation. The initial distribution is hot along $v_y$ and cold along $v_x$; the Weibel mode converts that anisotropy into magnetic energy, and by saturation the distribution is visibly rounder. This is the free-energy source being consumed, seen directly.](figures/vlasov_weibel_velocity.svg){#fig-vm-weibel-v}

The Weibel instability saturates differently, and the difference is
physical rather than numerical. There is no potential well to trap in; the
magnetic field grows until it is strong enough to deflect the counter-
streaming particles — magnetic trapping — and simultaneously the
anisotropy that drives it is eaten. @fig-vm-weibel-v shows the second
mechanism directly: the velocity distribution begins strongly elongated
along $v_y$ and ends visibly rounder.

The energy bookkeeping makes the same statement numerically. Through
saturation the magnetic energy rises by four orders of magnitude while the
kinetic energy falls by the same amount in absolute terms, and the
**total** is conserved to $8.6\times10^{-4}$ relative over 8000 steps. Only
the sum is conserved, and only because the exchange between the two is the
instability.

## Scaling {#sec-vm-scaling}

A fixed $128 \times 512 \times 512$ phase space — 33.6 million cells,
268 MB per working copy per species — on LUMI `standard`.

| ranks | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| wall (s) | 27.73 | 14.07 | 8.15 | 5.11 |
| speed-up | 1.00 | 1.97 | 3.40 | 5.43 |
| efficiency | — | 98.6 % | 85.1 % | 67.8 % |

: Strong scaling at fixed problem size. {#tbl-vm-scaling}

The ladder stops at 64 because of a limit this application states in
advance rather than discovers: with the decomposition on $v_y$ alone and a
halo of 6, the **rank cap is $N_{v_y}/\mathrm{halo} = 85$**. Going past it
needs a second decomposition axis and a transpose, which is a larger change
than the application justifies, and the constructor refuses rather than
silently producing a slab thinner than its own halo.

The falling efficiency is the moment reduction: it is an `MPI_Allreduce` of
$4N_x + 5$ doubles every step, so its cost is flat in the rank count while
the work per rank halves. That is the expected shape, and it is the reason
the decomposition was put on $v_y$ in the first place — the alternative,
decomposing $x$, would have made the *transport* communicate instead, which
is $N_xN_{v_x}N_{v_y}$ rather than $N_x$.

Transport bitwise agreement (1-rank vs N-rank `advect_vy`) is necessary
and not sufficient. `test_mpi_science` compares the fitted Landau
damping rate $\gamma$ of an identical $32^3$, $t=12$ run on
`MPI_COMM_SELF` against `MPI_COMM_WORLD`. The oracle is the 1-rank
$\gamma$, not the dispersion root. A parallel bug that shifted every
rank the same way would still match kinetic theory and fail this test.
On two ranks (job `21942462`, LUMI `debug`) both communicators give
$\gamma = -0.1514064581$, agreeing to the $10^{-8}$ relative tolerance.
NaN agreement is not a pass: the 1-rank rate is required to be finite
first.

### GPU

The device port was decided by measurement in two rounds rather than by
porting what looked expensive.

On the host at $256^3$, the two velocity shifts and the moment reduction
were 37 %, 15 % and 30 % of the step, the spectral $x$-shift 9 %, and the
field solve 0.01 %. Porting the first three took the step from 1.036 s to
0.127 s — and inverted the profile: the host $x$-shift was then 77 % and
the four whole-brick bus crossings it forced another 19 %. Only then was
the $x$-shift worth moving, with hipFFT, which keeps the brick resident on
the GCD for a whole step:

| phase space | host | one MI250X GCD | speed-up |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $128^3$ | — | — | 93.8× |
| $256^3$ | 1036 ms | 6.6 ms | **156.7×** |
| $128\times256\times256$ | — | — | 146.9× |

Two things were deliberately **not** ported, with the numbers that say so:
the 1-D field solve (0.13 ms/step, 1.9 % of the device step — the kernel
launches alone would cost that), and GPU-aware MPI for the velocity halo
(0.02 ms/step). Reporting a port that was not worth doing is part of the
measurement.

CPU–GPU parity passes in six configurations — 1/4/8 ranks, interpolation
orders 3/5/7, $N_x$ = 32/48/64. The tolerances are derived from the
arithmetic rather than fitted: $p\,u\max|f|$ for a $p$-point gather,
$8\log_2(N)\,u\sqrt{N}\max|f|$ for the transform, $2N_v u\kappa$ for the
reduction. The worst case used 0.006 % of its budget, and all three
transport operators differ by exactly **one ulp**. They are not bitwise
because the host build contracts `row += w*f` into an FMA while the kernels
do not — which is reported rather than papered over.

Operator parity is not a science rate. `vlasov_hip_parity --science=landau`
runs the same $32^3$, $t=12$ Landau problem on the host `Stepper` and
on `DeviceStepper` and compares `fit_envelope_rate` of `mode_ex`. That
test is registered as `vlasov-hip-science-rate` (HIP builds, LUMI-G).
Job `21943612` on one MI250X GCD measured
$\gamma_\mathrm{cpu}=\gamma_\mathrm{hip}=-0.1514064581$
(relative difference $6.0\times10^{-13}$), the same 1-rank Landau rate as
the CPU 1-vs-N check (job `21942462`). Operator parity remains job
`21933310` and is a different question.

## Limitations {#sec-vm-limits}

1. **Non-relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell is formally inconsistent.** Galilean
   particle dynamics with Lorentz-covariant fields is not a covariant
   theory. It is standard practice in the Weibel literature at modest
   drifts, and the runs here use $v/c \le 0.2$ with thermal spreads of
   0.05, but it is an approximation and not a small-parameter expansion
   anyone has controlled here.
2. **1D2V admits no oblique modes.** Every wave vector is along $x$. Real
   Weibel turbulence is a competition between obliquely propagating modes,
   and that competition is absent by construction.
3. **Velocity truncation and the spacing criterion.** The box must hold the
   distribution *and* the grid must integrate it; @eq-vm-quad is the second
   condition and it is now enforced, but both are conditions on a finite
   grid representing an infinite velocity space.
4. **Filamentation is unbounded and the grid is not.** Past saturation the
   solution develops structure below any fixed $\Delta v$. The entropy
   drift measures the loss; it does not repair it. Nothing in this chapter
   should be read as a converged late-time result.
5. **Recurrence, now measured.** A velocity grid of spacing $\Delta v$
   reconstructs its initial state at $T_R = 2\pi/(k\Delta v)$. That is a
   discrete-velocity fact, isolated here by streaming a Landau density
   perturbation with the self-consistent field off, so only the exact
   $x$-shift moves. Cell-centred $v_j = -v_{\max}+(j+\tfrac12)\Delta v$
   puts a global minus sign on the signed mode at $t=T_R$; the
   observable is $|\hat\rho|$.

   | $N_{v_x}$ | $\Delta v$ | $T_R^\mathrm{pred}$ | $T_R^\mathrm{meas}$ | ratio |
   |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
   | 24 | 0.033333 | 18.849556 | 18.849556 | 1.0000 |
   | 32 | 0.025000 | 25.132741 | 25.132743 | 1.0000 |
   | 48 | 0.016667 | 37.699112 | 37.699112 | 1.0000 |

   : Recurrence time against $T_R = 2\pi/(k\Delta v)$ at three velocity
   resolutions. Landau box, $v_{th}=0.05$, $v_{\max}=8v_{th}$,
   $k=k_\mathrm{skin}(1)$, $N_x=32$, $N_{v_y}=16$, streaming,
   `self_consistent=false`. {#tbl-vm-recurrence}

   The slope of $T_\mathrm{meas}$ against $1/\Delta v$ is $0.628319$
   against $2\pi/k = 0.628319$.
   A science-rate window that includes $t > 0.8\,T_R$ throws rather
   than quoting a recycled seed as a damping rate. The driver prints
   $T_R$ and $t_\mathrm{end}/T_R$ on rank 0 and does not auto-extend
   $t_\mathrm{end}$ past recurrence.
6. **Collisionless, non-relativistic, no ionisation, no Boltzmann
   operator.** Mobile ions exist behind a flag and are untested at scale.
7. **The rank cap of $N_{v_y}/\mathrm{halo}$**, as above.
8. **The transverse dispersion relation is derived here, not quoted.** Its
   provenance is the derivation, two analytic limits and the scan in
   @tbl-vm-weibel. That is stronger than a citation nobody can read, but it
   is not the same as a citation.

## Why this one is different

Every other application in this report evolves a field over physical space.
This one evolves a distribution over a phase space of higher dimension than
the space its fields live in, and that changes what is hard. It is not
another PDE on the same kind of unknown. What none of the other fourteen
applications demonstrate, and what this one has to get simultaneously
right, is:

- a distribution on a **three-dimensional phase-space grid**, not a
  physical-space field;
- **self-consistent Maxwell coupling** through kinetic moments, so the
  plasma lives in its own field;
- a **real Lorentz cross product**, which is why there are two velocity
  coordinates and why a magnetic field can grow from a noise seed;
- **electromagnetic instabilities** (Weibel / filamentation) that an
  electrostatic reduction cannot produce;
- Gauss's law as a **charge-conserving diagnostic**, preserved if and only
  if the transport and the deposition agree, not imposed as a constraint.

The individual operators are trivial — first-order advection, three of
them, each a translation along one axis. There is no $\nabla^8$ anywhere.
What is hard is that the unknown does not live where the fields live, so
every step crosses between them: the distribution is reduced to moments,
the moments drive the fields, the fields advect the distribution. Get the
reduction wrong by a transposed index and the code deposits a plausible
charge density for a different plasma. Get the velocity spacing wrong by a
factor of two and every rate is a per cent off in a way no scan of the
other axis can see.

And it is the one chapter where the governing system is genuinely large:
one kinetic equation per species on a three-dimensional phase space, the
Maxwell curls and the Lorentz force written in full before any reduction
(@eq-vm-vlasov–@eq-vm-moments), four surviving field components after a
reduction that has to be *derived*, two constraints of which one is free
and one is a diagnostic, and the moment integrals that close the loop.
@eq-vm-vlasov to @eq-vm-charge are what the code solves, and the reduction
from the first to the last is the part worth reading twice.
